jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 7 on the subalternation of theology, cross-referencing Aquinas, ST I q.1 a.2.

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e115.summary: Transition: having treated theology's causes, the Prologue now compares theology with other sciences.
concepts: comparison of theology with other sciences

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e124.summary: Divides the comparison into whether theology is subalternated to the science of the blessed and whether it is subalternated to, or subalternates, a humanly devised science. First argument for subalternation to the blessed: theology necessarily depends on their science, since we know supernatural things only as revealed by God and by the blessed who see what we believe.
claims: Theology depends on the knowledge of God and the blessed for its contents (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e151.summary: Second argument: as visual line is to line absolutely, so God as Saviour is to God absolutely; optics, about the visual line, is subalternated to geometry, so theology, about God as Saviour, is subalternated to the blessed's science of God absolutely.
claims: By analogy with optics and geometry, theology of God as Saviour is subalternate to the science of God absolutely (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e169.summary: Third argument: where one science's end is under another's (bridle-making and horsemanship, Ethics I), there is subalternation; theology's end, whether wayfarer's speculation or meritorious work, is ordered to heavenly contemplation.
claims: Theology's end is ordered to heavenly contemplation, so it is subalternated to the blessed's science (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e185.summary: Contrary argument: subalternating and subalternated sciences coexist and confirm each other (geometry and optics, arithmetic and music), but wayfarers' theology and the blessed's science cannot coexist. Response begins with what subalternation is: one science placed under another, not as particular under universal (as all sciences fall under science in general), nor by rank of dignity (from nobility of subject or certainty, as De anima vs. geometry), but by dependence of cognition, which may stem from the knower or from the knowable. Dependence from the knower arises from an individual's incapacity (believing a geometer) or from the common state (knowing only from sensibles, so needing revelation from those in another state).
claims: Subalternating and subalternated sciences can coexist in one person
Subalternation is not ordering of universal to particular nor ranking by dignity
Subalternation concerns dependence of cognition, from the knower's side or the knowable's

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e276.summary: No one bases subalternation on individual incapacity; some base it on dependence from the common state, but only to shore up the view that our theology is subalternated to the saints' science.
claims: Dependence from the knower's state is invoked only to support the subalternation of theology to the blessed's science

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e292.summary: Rejects this as frivolous: in the common state all intellectual knowledge depends on sensation, so intellect would be subalternated to sense; and the blessed's science would be subalternated to God's—which no one says.
claims: Dependence due to the knower's state does not cause subalternation
Otherwise intellectual cognition would be subalternated to sensation

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e312.summary: Only dependence from the knowable causes subalternation, where subjects relate as part to whole or as cause to effect. Essential part–whole relations (animal and man, mobile body and mobile body toward form or place) yield an imperfect subalternation, as De caelo and De generatione to Physics, since ignorance of the more known common features entails ignorance of the particulars. It is not perfect, because in perfect subalternation the higher science gives the propter quid of the lower's principles, whereas a genus gives neither the quia nor the propter quid of what is proper to its species, being essentially one with it.
claims: Only dependence from the side of the knowable causes subalternation
Subjects related as essential whole and subjective part yield only imperfect subalternation
In perfect subalternation the higher science gives the propter quid of the lower's principles
A genus cannot demonstrate propter quid anything of its species, being one with it in essence

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e422.summary: Reports the view that part 'in mode' (e.g. visual line relative to line) can yield perfect subalternation, since quantity in the visual line is cause of contingent features of seeing (things look larger or smaller by the angle), so geometry gives the propter quid of optics.
claims: Some hold that optics is subalternated to geometry as part in mode to whole (opinion)

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e453.summary: Rejects the account: optics' subject is not the coloured line but vision or the mode of seeing, and the properties it concludes (appearing larger, nearer, inverted) belong to the vision, not to the line; quantity is their efficient, not subjective, cause. So optics is not subalternated to geometry as part in mode to whole.
claims: The subject of optics is vision or the mode of seeing, not the coloured line
Quantity is an efficient, not subjective, cause of the properties of vision
Optics is not subalternated to geometry by part-in-mode relation of subjects

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e512.summary: Concludes that proper subalternation occurs only when the subjects are entirely distinct things ordered as end and means (bridle and riding: horsemanship gives the propter quid of the bridle's form) or as effect and efficient cause (medicine and natural philosophy: the natural philosopher explains why rhubarb purges choler). These are the only two modes of proper subalternation.
claims: Proper subalternation occurs only between sciences whose subjects relate as end and means or as effect and efficient cause
Subalternation by end is found chiefly in practical sciences and arts

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e560.summary: Main answer: though our theology depends on the science of God and the blessed because of our state as wayfarers, it is not properly subalternated to it in any of these modes, since the blessed's science does not give the propter quid of what faith and theology hold as quia: some articles have no cause (the Trinity), and those that do (incarnation, passion, for our salvation) have a propter quid our theology states equally well, not received from the blessed.
claims: Theology is not properly subalternated to the science of the blessed
The blessed's science supplies no propter quid of theology's principles beyond what theology itself holds
Some articles, like the Trinity, have no cause; others have salvation as their cause, which theology already states

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e612.summary: Reply to the first argument: dependence from the knower does not suffice for subalternation; dependence from the knowable is required, such that the higher science gives the propter quid of the lower's principles. Theology depends on the blessed's science only in the first way.
claims: Theology depends on the blessed's science only from the side of the knower

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e632.summary: Reply to the second: the analogy fails because the line has properties known to geometry that cause differences in seeing, whereas God has no property causing our salvation other than his will ('he saved me because he willed me', Ps 17), and theology holds this of itself, not from the blessed.
claims: God's will is the only cause of our salvation
Theology knows that cause itself, not from the science of the blessed
concepts: divine will as cause of salvation

jsnvu6-d1e155-d1e666.summary: Reply to the third: helping another's end does not suffice for subalternation (else moral sciences, which calm the passions for contemplation, would be subalternated to all speculative sciences); the lower science's subject must be ordered to the higher's as end and used by it for its own end, as bridle to riding and riding to warfare. Wayfarer's speculation is not theology's subject, and the blessed's science does not use meritorious work, which does not exist in the blessed life, so it gives no propter quid about it.
claims: Subalternation requires the lower subject to be ordered to and used by the higher science
The blessed's science does not use meritorious works, so practical theology is not subalternated to it

jsnvu6-d1e155.summary: Question 7 opens the Prologue's comparison of theology with other sciences by asking whether our theology is subalternated to the science of the blessed. Durandus first analyzes subalternation: it is neither universal-particular ordering nor ranking by dignity, but dependence of cognition; dependence on the knower's side (individual incapacity or the common state of knowing from sensibles) does not suffice, else intellect would be subalternate to sense. Only dependence from the knowable counts: essential whole–part relations of subjects yield only imperfect subalternation (a genus gives no propter quid of its species); the alleged part-in-mode case of optics and geometry fails since optics concerns vision, of which quantity is only an efficient cause; proper subalternation obtains only when subjects relate as end and means (bridle-making and horsemanship) or effect and efficient cause (medicine and natural philosophy). Hence theology, though it depends on God's and the blessed's knowledge because of our state, is not properly subalternated to the blessed's science, which supplies no propter quid for theology's principles: the Trinity has no cause, and the cause of the saving mysteries—God's will for our salvation—theology knows of itself; nor does the blessed's science use meritorious works.
claims: Subalternation requires dependence of cognition from the side of the knowable, not the knower
Proper subalternation occurs only when subjects relate as end and means or effect and efficient cause
Theology is not properly subalternated to the science of the blessed
The blessed's science supplies no propter quid of theology's principles
concepts: God's will as cause of salvation
